description: The web server serves the .git directory (source control metadata) directly, allowing the entire repository — including full commit history — to be reconstructed and downloaded by anyone who can reach the site.
impact: Full source code disclosure, including any credentials, API keys, or internal comments ever committed to the repository, even if later removed in a subsequent commit — git history retains everything unless the repository was rewritten.
remediation: Remove or block web-server access to the .git directory entirely (deny access at the web server/reverse-proxy config level).
Never deploy by copying a working directory that includes .git into the web root — use a proper build/deploy pipeline that excludes it.
If a .git directory was ever exposed, treat every credential and secret that ever appeared in the repository's history as compromised and rotate it.

audience_guidance.student: .git is the hidden folder Git uses to track a project's full history. If a web server accidentally serves that folder, tools can reconstruct the entire codebase — including old versions that might still contain a password someone forgot to remove.
audience_guidance.developer: Deploy from a build artifact that never includes .git, and add an explicit deny rule for .git at the web server config level as defense in depth.
audience_guidance.bug_bounty_hunter: Check for /.git/HEAD or /.git/config directly; if reachable, tools like git-dumper can pull the full repository for offline analysis — always worth a look for hardcoded secrets in history.
audience_guidance.pentester: Dump the exposed repository and search its full commit history (not just the latest commit) for credentials, internal hostnames, and comments revealing further attack surface.
audience_guidance.security_team: Scan externally-facing hosts for exposed .git directories as a routine check, and treat any find as an immediate incident requiring full secret rotation, not just removing the folder.
